title: Closed-loop control with PID
summary: A PID controller measures the process value, compares it with the setpoint and adjusts the output until they match. Its proportional, integral and derivative parts each have a job, and its limits and manual mode matter as much as its gains.

sections.heading: Open loop and closed loop
sections.body: Switching a heater on for a fixed time is **open-loop** control: nothing checks whether the vessel actually got warm. A **closed loop** measures the process value (**PV**, here the temperature), compares it with the setpoint (**SP**) and adjusts the manipulated variable (**MV**, here the heater power) until the error SP - PV is gone. A PID controller is the most common way to compute MV from the error.

sections.heading: Proportional action
sections.body: The **P** part is the gain **KP** times the error: a large error gives a large output. P alone always leaves an **offset**: the heater only works while there is an error. In PLC Lab's vessel, KP 4 settles at about 50.5 °C instead of 60 °C. A larger KP shrinks the offset but makes the loop nervous and, with process lag, makes it oscillate.

sections.heading: Integral action
sections.body: The **I** part adds up the error over time, so it keeps growing until the error is zero: it removes the offset. The integral time **TI** says how fast: after TI with a constant error, I has grown as large as P. A short TI acts fast but overshoots; a long TI is calm but slow. In the steady state the whole output comes from I.

sections.heading: Derivative action
sections.body: The **D** part reacts to how fast the measurement changes and brakes the output before the PV reaches the setpoint. The derivative time **TD** sets its strength. PLC Lab's PID differentiates the measurement, not the error, so a setpoint step gives no jump in D. Real measurements are noisy and D amplifies noise, which is why many loops run as PI.

sections.heading: Limits, windup and manual mode
sections.body: A heater cannot deliver more than 100 % or less than 0 %. While MV sits at a limit, an integral that kept growing would **wind up** and cause a large overshoot later. PLC Lab's PID stops integrating while the output is saturated (SAT is TRUE). In **manual** mode the operator sets MV_MAN directly; the integral follows it, so switching back to automatic continues from the manual output without a jump (**bumpless transfer**).

sections.heading: Tuning in practice
sections.body: Start with P only and raise KP until the loop reacts briskly without oscillating. Then add I with a TI close to the slowest time constant of the process and shorten it while the overshoot stays acceptable. Watch the trend of SP, PV and MV: a PV that swings around SP means too much gain or too short a TI; an MV that sits at a limit means the actuator is too small for the request. Dead time limits how fast any controller can be.

sections.heading: The PID block in PLC Lab
sections.body:
PID is a standard function block of the PLC runtime, called like TON:

```
Loop(SP := Setpoint, PV := Temperature, KP := 3.0, TI := T#20s,
     MANUAL := NOT AutoMode, MV_MAN := 25.0, MV => Heater);
```

Its outputs MV, E, P, I, D and SAT appear online under the instance name, for example `Loop.I`. It runs on the simulated task time and gives the same result on every computer. It is a generic educational controller; vendor PID blocks differ in names, units and algorithms.
